claims.text: Resistance of high-entropy alloys to simultaneous wear and corrosion is primarily governed by the rapid self-healing of their passive films after mechanical rupture.
Rapid passive-film healing maintains an intact surface barrier.
An intact passive-film barrier minimizes mechanical abrasion.
An intact passive-film barrier minimizes electrochemical attack.
The initial HEA surfaces possess a potential passive film.
Controlled heat treatment or surface pre-modification can enhance or diminish passive-film healing kinetics.
Surface modification or heat treatment changes the structural integrity and healing kinetics of the self-forming passive oxide film.
A passive film that remains intact or rapidly repairs after mechanical damage acts as a barrier to wear.
A passive film that remains intact or rapidly repairs after mechanical damage acts as a barrier to corrosion.
Degradation accelerates once the passive film is compromised.
Passive-film healing mediates a synergistic reduction of degradation under combined mechanical and corrosive stress.
HEA variants engineered for faster passive-film healing will exhibit lower combined tribocorrosion degradation than a matched baseline without enhanced healing.
For faster-healing HEAs, combined degradation will be less than the additive effects measured in independent wear-only and corrosion-only tests.
Differences between faster-healing and baseline HEAs will be less pronounced in isolated wear-only or corrosion-only tests than in combined tribocorrosion tests.
The predicted protection applies when passive-film repair can keep pace with mechanical disruption and corrosive attack.
The protective effect may be negated when passive-film destruction overwhelmingly exceeds the healing rate.
Quantitative improvement and the threshold at which film healing becomes ineffective depend on alloy composition and testing conditions.
